  This example paper demonstrates the paper-handler workflow. It shows how a

## Introduction

A paper is easier to trust when its source is available and its build is
repeatable. That principle motivates treating the manuscript as a small software
project rather than a binary attachment [@doe2024]. The PDF becomes an output,
while the text, citations and data remain reviewable inputs.

This example exercises that idea on a deliberately small document. It is also
the regression fixture for the repository: the render check builds it with the
same pinned toolchain that a reader would use.

## Related Work

Earlier work on reproducible writing emphasises plain-text sources and automated
builds [@roe2021]. This example follows that advice and adds a narrow constraint:
the toolchain itself is pinned, so a missing font or a newer TeX distribution
cannot silently change the output.

## Method

Each paper is a directory with one entry document, a bibliography and any
figures or data it needs. A small command renders the entry document from inside
that directory, so relative paths resolve the way an author expects.

The workflow keeps a short feedback loop:

$$
\text{write} \rightarrow \text{lint} \rightarrow \text{render}.
$$

The lint step checks structure and prose before the slower render step runs. It
reports placeholders, heading jumps, undefined citations and overlong sentences.

## Results

The example renders without network access once the toolchain is present. Table
1 summarises the three steps.

| Step | Input | Output |
|------|-------|--------|
| Write | `index.qmd` | edited source |
| Lint | source + `references.bib` | diagnostics |
| Render | source | `index.pdf` |

: The three-step writing loop.

## Discussion

Pinning the toolchain removes one common source of irreproducibility, but it
does not remove every source. Data files can still change, and a citation can
still point at the wrong paper. The workflow makes those problems visible rather
than invisible, which is the practical benefit.

A second benefit is reviewability. A diff shows exactly which sentences and
citations changed, so a co-author can review the argument rather than a rebuilt
PDF.

## Conclusion

This example shows that a small amount of build infrastructure can make an
academic manuscript reproducible. The same approach scales to a journal
template: the source stays plain text, and the toolchain stays pinned.
